title: Bid, Ask, and the Hidden Cost of a Trade

cards.headline: There is never one price. There are always two.
cards.body: Look up a stock and you see a single number. That number is history — the last trade that happened. Right now the market is quoting two prices: the most any buyer will pay, and the least any seller will take. You trade against one of them, never the middle.

cards.headline: One quote, two numbers.
cards.body: Say a company is quoted 10.00 bid, 10.04 ask. The **bid** is the highest price a buyer is willing to pay. The **ask** is the lowest price a seller will accept. The four cents between them is the **spread**.

cards.headline: You pay it coming and going.
cards.body: Buy 100 shares and you pay the ask: 1,004 dollars. Change your mind a second later and sell at the bid: 1,000 dollars. Nothing moved. You are down four dollars, or **0.4 percent**, before the market has done anything at all.

cards.prompt: A stock is quoted 10.00 bid, 10.04 ask. You buy, then sell one second later with no change in the quote. Where do you stand?

options.label: Break even — the price never moved
Down 0.4 percent, paid to the spread

cards.explanation: You bought at the ask and sold at the bid. The quote never moved, but you crossed the spread twice. That four cents is a **real cost** — it simply never appears as a line item on your statement.

cards.headline: Liquidity sets the width.
cards.body: Spreads are narrow where trading is heavy. A stock trading millions of shares a day may be quoted a penny wide. A stock that trades a few thousand shares a day can sit fifty cents wide, or more. Fewer buyers and sellers, bigger gap.

cards.title: A thin market, quoted wide
cards.caption: This stock trades a few thousand shares a day. The best bid sits at 49.60, the best ask at 50.40 — eighty cents apart. A round trip costs you 1.6 percent.

cards.body: The more shares that change hands each day, the narrower the spread tends to be. That depth of buying and selling interest is called [[1]].
cards.explanation: Liquidity is how easily you can trade size without moving the price. Deep liquidity means many competing buyers and sellers, and that competition squeezes the spread down to pennies.

cards.title: The cost of trading often
cards.caption: A 0.4 percent spread sounds like nothing. Pay it once a year and it is. Pay it every week and you give up close to a fifth of your capital in spread alone.

cards.summary: Every stock has two live prices. The gap between them is a cost you pay on every round trip, and nobody itemises it.
bullets: You buy at the ask and sell at the bid — never in between.
Heavily traded stocks quote pennies apart; thinly traded ones can quote dollars apart.
The spread is charged per trade, so frequency multiplies it.

cards.insight: The market never quotes you one price. It quotes two, and the distance between them is the toll you pay for changing your mind.
